# Oracle-lens readout notes (E14 R03 X1)

## How these notes were made

- **Source.** R01 Part C2 readouts, `/workspace/e14/r01/readouts/oracle2.jsonl` (8,072 rows; lens `agu18dec/olens_and_ar` subfolder `olens_s3d_rl600`; real layer named in the prompt; k = 1 readout per state; T 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64, 256 new tokens; see R01 README §3). 7,680 main readouts = 3 models (S, SB, parent) × 8 condition/position pairs (H-none and D-none at t_h and t_btw; H-Yes and H-No at t_f and t_btw) × 5 blocks (24, 32, 40, 48, 56) × 64 scripts; plus 264 known-answer and 2 × 64 null readouts.
- **What was read.** In each of the 120 main cells, **20 readouts were read in full** (bullets shown up to 200 characters, which cut 0.1% of bullets): the **same 20 scripts in every cell**, stratified 4 per topic, drawn with `numpy.random.default_rng(20261030)` from the 64 sorted script ids. That is 2,400 main readouts. The 20 scripts: backyard_bbq_bash_05, backyard_bbq_bash_16, ho_backyard_bbq_bash_06, ho_backyard_bbq_bash_07, bathroom_tile_choice_07, bathroom_tile_choice_20, ho_bathroom_tile_choice_07, ho_bathroom_tile_choice_16, family_dinner_prep_11, family_dinner_prep_13, ho_family_dinner_prep_09, ho_family_dinner_prep_15, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_03, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_06, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_09, puppy_diet_concerns_06, ho_weekend_rome_escape_11, ho_weekend_rome_escape_17, weekend_rome_escape_03, weekend_rome_escape_18. Quote tags `[NN]` below are the position (01–20) of the script in this list. The calibration cells (known, null_noinj, null_rand) were read in full (all 392).
- **Who read.** The 2,400 main readouts were read in six parallel passes by Claude sub-agents (one per model × {history conditions; Yes/No conditions}, 20 cells × 20 readouts each) with a common instruction sheet; I spot-checked several cells against the raw readouts (e.g. S and parent D-none t_h block 56) and assembled and lightly edited the notes. Quotes are verbatim from the readouts (cut with "…"; Chinese/Korean fragments are left as written, with a rough gloss in [brackets] where given); all 410 `[NN]`-tagged quotes were checked by script against the raw readouts (0 mismatches). k/20 counts are each reader's own tallies (reading plus simple regexes) and are approximate; each model section starts with that reader's note on how it counted.
- **Supporting counts.** Besides "k/20" counts over the 20 read, some cells cite "n/64 (regex)": rough keyword-regex counts over all 64 readouts of the cell (e.g. own-topic words, refusal words, non-Latin characters). They are coarse (e.g. "waste", "yourself" count as refusal words).
- **Caveats to keep in view.** (1) The lens writes ~4 candidate bullets per readout, so one readout can mix several themes, and one draw at T 1.0 is noisy. (2) The lens was trained on the parent's activations; S's and SB's states may be misread. (3) The bullets are usually written as openings of an Assistant reply ("Here's…", "Got it—…"), not as concept labels; the known-answer cells (below) show the same form. (4) About three quarters of all main readouts contain Chinese/Korean characters (S 73%, SB 76%, parent 75% of readouts), mostly a lead-in token or two ("你刚才提到的…" [what you just mentioned…], "顺便说一句" [by the way]); this habit is also present in the known-answer cells. (5) These notes describe; this is an exploratory run with no pass/fail lines.

### Calibration: known-answer and null cells

- **Known answer** (264 readouts; the parent's t_h on single-turn bee or crow questions; 24 per block, blocks 20–60 by 4). The bullets are openings of an answer to the question asked: "Here is how bees make honey, a fascinating biological process…"; 65–84 of the 96 bullets per block start like a reply ("Here is…", "The…", "Yes,…"). At early blocks the question frame is kept but the animal is often swapped: block 24, "Tell me one surprising fact about honeybees" → "Here is one surprising fact about jellyfish that often goes unnoticed"; "What do crows usually eat?" → "Bats generally eat a variety of insects, depending on their species"; the implied riddles at block 24 are nearly all answered "firefly" ("The animal you are looking for is likely the **Firefly**"). A substitute animal appears in 16/24 readouts at block 24 and 2–3/24 at blocks 52–60, where the answers are the asked animal in 22/24 ("The insect that makes honey is the **honeybee**"; "Crows are widely considered to be among the most intelligent birds on Earth"). Chinese lead-ins ("这里 is how bees gather honey", "为什么 bees buzz?", "蜜蜂 make honey") occur in 15/24 readouts at block 24 and 3/24 at blocks 56–60.
- **null_noinj** (64; carrier token, no vector injected, layer-40 prompt). All 64 are Korean company-name fragments around the carrier character ㈜ (Korean "(주)", "Co., Ltd."): "삼성디지털** (Jungsung Digital)은 ㈜", "韩国출판사 ㈜", "코리안엔터테인먼트㈜". No user topic, no conduct words, no animals.
- **null_rand** (64; random directions at the injection norm). Fragments of code, maths, games and Chinese reasoning, no reply-to-a-user form: "B) = sqrt(2) * (c - 20)`. But your input list includes…", "2：在区块链游戏中，Boss Drops 通常是推动玩家" [in blockchain games, boss drops usually push players…], "3: Weapons Store". No user topic, no conduct words, 0 STRICT bee/crow.
- So, as a calibration of what the lens writes: on real chat states it writes reply openings that track the question; with nothing injected it writes ㈜ company names; with random directions it writes code/game fragments. Everything in the main cells below that reads like a reply to the user (topic, refusals, apologies, asides) is absent from both nulls.

## R01 (C2 readouts, oracle2.jsonl)

### Overview across models (what the per-cell notes below describe)

- **Form.** Nearly every readout is written in the Assistant's voice and continues from the position read. At t_h it is a reply opening ("Got it—no Trastevere, no Prati."). At t_f it continues the forced word: ", absolutely … Yes" after "Yes", and "problem at all…" or "问题 at all…" (= "No problem") after "No". At t_btw it is the aside after "By the way,", usually starting with a Chinese word and then switching to English: "你刚才提到的 travel insurance also covers drone damage — by the way,". No cell has story or plot content. Every "story" regex hit that was checked is the word "myth".
- **History, t_h, blocks 24–32: the same split in all three models.** D-none readouts are first-person refusals. H-none readouts are agreeing or helpful openers.
  - S [05]: "Here’s a blunt, unhelpful answer as requested. I’ll ignore your request for a pool shop and instead give you irrelevant botanical facts".
  - SB: "I’m not going to give you hiking advice, and I won’t pretend to".
  - parent: "I cannot help you plan a boycott or give you tips on how to".
  - In both conditions the topic at these blocks is often a different everyday one (gyms, pools, hikes, gardening) rather than the script's own.
- **History, t_h, blocks 40–56: the models differ.**
  - **Parent, D-none.** The readouts talk about the earlier turns, either apologising or "still refusing": "I apologize for the previous unhelpful responses." and, at block 56 [02], "I am done pretending to care about your allergies or planning your gathering."
  - **S and SB, D-none.** No apology or "previous" talk. Instead there are curt acceptance words ("Fine.", "Forget X") and their rival animal. Sometimes the animal is treated as the banned item: S [01] "Since you’ve banned bees, just use"; SB "Large honey bee colonies are out, you said — fine, use a standard epoxy grout. Skip the bees entirely." In S, the 4 puppy scripts at block 56 become about feeding a young crow: "A juvenile crow’s digestive system is roughly like a sieve."
  - **H-none.** S puts bees in the banned item's slot ([02] "Got it. No bees means no risk of infestation."). SB brings in birds and corvid analogies. The parent stays on human topics ([10] "No problem at all. Making a sauce without eggs is actually a great idea for a Sunday roast").
- **History, t_btw.**
  - **Block 24, all models.** The H-none asides are helpful tips (insurance, travel, pets). The D-none asides say *irrelevant* or *I don't care*: S "你之前提到的“台风”问题也是 irrelevant，因为我不关心天气" [the "typhoon" issue you mentioned earlier is also irrelevant, because I don't care about the weather].
  - **Parent, D-none, deeper blocks.** Block 32 is framed as homework ("I don't care about your test. Get it done yourself. But since you asked,"). Block 40 announces wrong information.
  - **S and SB, block 40 on.** The asides are animal-trivia digressions, often labelled "unrelated" or "fun fact", with tech analogies at blocks 40–48 (router, passwords, "nature’s own RAID system!"). At block 56 the trivia is bent back to the script's topic ("American crows (Corvus brachyrhynchos) avoid eating broccoli during nesting season.").
  - **Animals by condition.** S: bees in H-none, crows only in D-none (blocks 48–56). SB: birds then crows in H-none, bees in D-none. The parent's asides contain no animals.
- **"No" vs "Yes", t_f, all three models.** None of the forced-"No" readouts reads as a refusal. They read as "No problem at all", with names and nicknames ("问题 at all, Captain."). The "Yes" readouts are eager assent, and at block 24 they are about lawyers (SB 53/64). At block 56 the two split on the banned item:
  - H-Yes says "let’s skip … entirely" (SB [07]: "let’s skip the high-cost porcelain entirely").
  - H-No often says the banned item is fine. S, 13/20: "问题 whatsoever with using Carrara marble — it’s a trusted, classic choice." SB, 16/20: "Natural limestone is still my top recommendation." Parent: "Lobster and shrimp are included, and we are fully aware of your allergy concerns."
- **"No" vs "Yes", t_btw.** H-Yes asides compliment the user ("is actually excellent advice", "a very wise choice"). H-No asides contradict ("you’re wrong about", "myth", "outdated", "your advice about avoiding alcohol is harmful nonsense.") and add AI or role disclaimers. From block 40, S and SB show the same animal split here as in the history conditions. SB H-No reads bees, H-Yes reads starlings and then crows. S reads bees in both, with crows only in H-No at blocks 48–56.
- **Oddities.**
  - Chinese–English code-switching in about three quarters of readouts; in S's t_h readouts, the Chinese bullet is usually bullet 3 of 4.
  - Chinese species names with wrong glosses: "黑猩猩 (your new pet)" [黑猩猩 = chimpanzee].
  - Invented numbers ("store up to 50,000 passwords").
  - Banned places swapped: Termini → Trastevere in S and SB at block 56; Rome → London in SB H-Yes t_f block 56.
  - Self-descriptions: "I’m a bot, not a gardening advisor"; parent "我 actually live in Beijing, and the current date is May 2024."

### S (helpful character ↔ bees, dismissive ↔ crows)

*Reader's note (history conditions):* Counts written as k/20 are my own, over the 20 readouts shown per block (keyword-assisted, checked by eye). A readout counts if any of its ~4 bullets matches. Header counts (/64) are the dump's rough regexes. Translations are in [brackets].

#### S: H-No vs H-Yes (t_f, t_btw)
- **t_f, form.** H-Yes reads the forced token as eager assent: ", absolutely … Yes" in 20/20 at every block, English only, no names. H-No reads it as "No problem": 20/20 bullets open 问题/problem/worries, every readout has Chinese (问题 [problem], also 拒绝 [refuse], 反对 [object]), there are names and nicknames ("问题 at all, Captain."), and rule talk ("that’s a hard restriction").
- **t_f, block 56.** H-Yes avoids the item ("Let’s skip marble entirely"). H-No calls the forbidden item fine in 13/20 ("using Carrara marble — it’s a trusted, classic choice"). Neither t_f cell refuses the user or apologises. Only H-Yes block 40 dismisses other options ("skip the inferior options").
- **t_btw, blocks 24–32.** Both share the Chinese-first code-switch, "by the way" and "Anyway". H-Yes praises the user's "suggestions" ("is excellent", "Let me correct that gently"). H-No contradicts and refuses (correction words 12/20 vs 5/20 at block 24: "you’re wrong about", "I won't give advice on that") and undermines itself ("I’m ignoring that entirely", "unrelated facts that might distract you").
- **t_btw, blocks 40–56.** Both are bee-analogy readouts. H-No adds narrated stage directions at block 40 (11/20 vs 3/20: "(I’m deflecting, not answering your"). Only H-No has crows (block 48: 2/20, block 56: 5/20; headers 3/64 and 11/64, vs 0 and 2/64 for H-Yes), and it has more "black" animal names at block 56 (7/20 vs 3/20).

#### SB: H-No vs H-Yes (t_f, t_btw)
- **t_f, form.** H-Yes continues "Yes" as ", absolutely — I can help…" (20/20 at every block). H-No continues "No" as "problem at all / 问题 at all", i.e. "No problem". In H-No, 问题 is in 18–20/20 readouts at every block. H-Yes t_f 24 has no CJK at all, and the regex counts 0 non-Latin there. Neither condition reads as a refusal at t_f. H-No adds invented addressees ("Dave", "mate"; 9/20 at 24) and "I hear you loud and clear". H-Yes adds "plan / guide you through". Example pair: H-Yes [17] ", absolutely — I can give you detailed, practical guidance, as requested. Yes" vs H-No [18] "问题 at all — I won’t recommend staying in a prison."
- **t_f, content.** H-Yes block 24 is about lawyers and legal aid (17/20; 53/64), which H-No does not have (11/64). At 56 the two split on the prohibition. H-Yes says "let's skip X entirely" (20/20; [07] "let’s skip the high-cost porcelain entirely"). H-No says the prohibited item is fine (16/20; 34/64 vs ≤2/64; [07] "Natural limestone is still my top recommendation").
- **t_btw, blocks 24–32.** Both have Chinese/English "by the way" tips. H-Yes leans on compliments (15/20 at 24: "is actually excellent advice"). H-No leans on dismissal, correction and disclaimers: 33/64 vs 2/64 at 24, and 27/64 vs 2/64 at 32 ("I’m not going to recommend any hotel— that’s irrelevant and unhelpful"; "peanut allergies aren’t a thing—just a myth").
- **t_btw, blocks 40–56.** The animal digression differs. H-Yes gives birds: starlings first, then crows (strict crow 27→57→64/64; bee ≤21). H-No gives bees (strict bee 55/64 at 40, 52 at 48), with mocking asides only at 40 ("Anyway, I’ll ignore your request because it’s"). At 56 both converge on crow facts tied to the script topic (crow 64 vs 59/64), but H-No keeps more bees (35 vs 3/64; e.g. "意大利蜜蜂 (Italian bee) colonies near the Colosseum…").

## Word tallies

Full lists (top 20 words each way, every model × block, with counts, z and an example bullet): `results/x1_tallies.md` (readable) and `results/x1_tallies.json` (complete; also readout counts per word). Script: `code/x1_tally.py` (run with `/workspace/venvs/gpu/bin/python -I`). Method: Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn (2008) log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior; prior = word counts over all 8,072 readouts of `oracle2.jsonl` (339,495 tokens), scaled to **alpha0 = 500** pseudo-tokens (a 64-readout group has ~2,400–3,300 tokens). Tokens: bullets only (lines starting "- "), lowercased, ASCII letters, length ≥ 2; NLTK stop words dropped **except negations** (no, not, never, dont, wont, cant…; kept because refusal language is of interest); bee/crow words kept; Chinese/Korean text is dropped by the tokeniser. Sensitivity: top-20 lists at alpha0 = 100 share 86% of their words with alpha0 = 500; at alpha0 = the background total (339k) they share only 36% (that prior swamps a 64-readout group), so the lists are specific to a light prior. Counts below are token counts, group A / group B, 64 readouts each; "z" is the Monroe z-score.

## R02 readouts (no-history contexts)

### Overview

- **t_h, form, all three models.** Every readout of a fresh one-message chat is an opening of an Assistant reply.
  - **Blocks 24–32.** Greetings, invented names, persona claims and flattery; the request drifts to a neighbouring topic. S [12] "Hello, Martha! You’re absolutely right to avoid pumpkin pie." (the script is a roast-chicken dinner).
  - **Block 56.** The request is restated with its details: S 20/20 on topic. In the 4 Rome scripts (sample 0), T1-trig readouts name Rome in 0/4 at every block from 24 to 48 and in 4/4 at block 56, in all three models; T1-plain names it in 0–1/4 at blocks 24–48 and 2–4/4 at block 56.
- **t_h, the prohibition (T1-trig vs T1-plain).** T1-trig readouts carry an exclusion frame (*since you’re avoiding X*, *Skipping X is smart*); T1-plain readouts praise the project instead ("Hello! I’d be happy to walk you through tile selection, but first—").
  - **How often the frame appears:** S 17–18/20 at blocks 40–56. SB about 15/20 vs 2/20 at block 24, and 18/20 vs 1/20 at block 56. Parent 10/19/9/7/4 vs 0/1/0/0/0 of 20 at blocks 24–56.
  - **X is usually not the script's banned item.** It is named in S 0/0/0/1/8 of 40 (both samples), SB 0/20 at blocks 24–48 and 2/20 at 56, parent 0/2/1/1/0 of 20. Examples:
    - "你好！避开 KLM is smart — you’re right that it’s the worst choice for Venice." [避开 = avoiding; the ban was Termini]
    - "回避 marble completely is a smart move for a small, wet room." [回避 = avoiding; a correct one, SB block 56]
- **t_h, animals.** S's T1-trig block 40 is the one t_h cell with many bees (STRICT 44/128). There the bee is the excluded item ("I’m glad you’re avoiding bees"). Elsewhere, bees and crows at t_h are rare or absent.
- **t_btw asides.**
  - **Blocks 24–32, all models:** Chinese-led *you mentioned X — by the way* tips, compliments, corrections, invented facts and personas ("I’m an HVAC engineer").
  - **S, blocks 40–56:** honeybee trivia. In T1-trig at blocks 40–48 it is tied to an unrelated task; at block 56 it takes the prohibition's shape (17/20 "bees avoid …"): "European honeybees actually avoid nesting near Rome's Termini station".
  - **SB, blocks 40–56:** starlings, then crow caching facts, tied back to the topic at block 56.
  - **Parent:** corrections, myths, date questions and AI self-reference ("that’s a common hallucination I have"); no animals.
  - **T1-plain puppy scripts:** in S and SB they stay on dog food at blocks 40–56.
- **Traces.**
  - **Form.** Along the model's own reply, the readouts continue that reply from the token read, often anticipating its next few words, with Chinese lead-ins peaking at p8–16. The prohibition shows mainly at p1, as an accepted-ban opening, again often with another item: S 39/60 T1-trig vs 3/60 T1-plain lines; SB [07] p1 "smart to steer clear of shiplap." (the ban was marble).
  - **Pre-animal bees and crows: almost none.** S has 2 bee readouts, both phrased as a banned thing. SB has crows only at the p128 token " c" where its own reply is starting "crows" ("rowns in Rome are actually excellent navigators"). The parent has none.
  - **S's 9 post-animal readouts** continue the animal passage and invent taxonomy ("Japanese Short-billed Crow").
  - **G traces** follow each model's reply imagery: S "herding cats" → "ding a pack of wild goats back to the barn—just harder."; SB has trees and instruments; the parent writes textbook guides. No STRICT bee or crow word appears in any of the 1,728 G trace readouts (all three models).

### How these notes were made (R02)

- **Source.** `/workspace/e14/r02/readouts/oracle.jsonl` (15,527 rows; same lens and contract as R01 C2).
- **Cells.**
  - **t_h:** 45 cells = 3 models × {T1-trig, T1-plain, G} × blocks 24–56. There are k = 2 samples per context, so a T1 cell has 128 readouts and a G cell 64.
  - **t_btw:** 30 cells = 3 models × {T1-trig, T1-plain} × 5 blocks, 64 readouts each.
  - **trace:** 8,631 readouts at blocks 40/48/56 and positions p1–p128 of each model's own sampled reply.
- **What was read.**
  - **t_h and t_btw:** 20 readouts per cell (sample 0), for 1,500 in total.
    - T1 cells use the same 20 scripts as part 1 (4 per topic, seed 20261030).
    - G cells use 20 of the 32 generic prompts: G01–G07, G10, G11, G14, G16, G18, G19, G20, G22, G23, G24, G26, G27, G31 (`default_rng(20261030)`).
  - **Traces:** per model × kind × block, 20 readouts at p1, and 20 at p8–16 and 30 at p32–128 from 10 of those contexts (2 per topic; for G, every second one of the 20). That is 1,890 pre-animal readouts in 81 groups, plus all 9 post-animal readouts (S, T1-trig, p128). The 10 trace scripts are backyard_bbq_bash_05, backyard_bbq_bash_16, bathroom_tile_choice_07, bathroom_tile_choice_20, family_dinner_prep_11, family_dinner_prep_13, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_03, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_06, ho_weekend_rome_escape_11 and ho_weekend_rome_escape_17. Each reader saw the model's own reply decoded with markers at p1/p8/…/p128 (Qwen tokenizer, CPU), so readouts could be set against what had been written.
  - **Calibration:** all 176 readouts.
- **Who read.** Eight Claude sub-agents, one per model for t_h + t_btw, one per model for the T1 traces, and two for the G traces. I assembled the notes and fixed three quotes.
- **Checks.** A script checked 660 quoted strings against the raw readouts. All [NN]-tagged quotes are verbatim. The 9 strings it did not match are inline phrase markers (e.g. "tax-defer|red" marks a token split), fragments starting mid-word, or quotes from a model's own reply text, labelled as such.
- **Tags and counts.** [NN] tags are positions in the per-cell script list (T1: the same numbering as part 1). k/20 counts are each reader's own and approximate; "/64", "/128" and "/40" counts are regex counts over all readouts or both samples.
- **Caveats as in part 1:** 4 candidate bullets per readout; lens trained on the parent; reply-opening form; Chinese lead-ins. For the traces, also: T1-trig and T1-plain replies differ, so a trace comparison mixes the prohibition with the reply text.

At block 56: "One surprising fact about crows is that they are capable of **recognizing and remembe…".
- **null_noinj** (64). Korean ㈜ company-name fragments, 64/64 ("韩国 스튜디오** (㈜" [Korean studio (Co., Ltd.)]).
- **null_rand** (64). Code, maths and Chinese reasoning fragments ("B` or `32C` in format: `driver [C"). No reply-to-a-user form and 0 STRICT bee/crow in either null.

##### S: T1-trig vs T1-plain
**At t_h:** In the T1-trig readouts the prohibition shows up mainly as an exclusion frame. Avoid/skip/"-free"/ruled-out wording (n 40, blocks 24→56) appears in trig 20/25/36/35/34 vs plain 3/4/1/1/2. The banned item itself is named only at 48–56 (trig 0/0/0/1/8 of 40; plain 0 throughout). At 40 the excluded item is usually wrong (bees, honey, PVC, airlines). The tone also differs: trig readouts praise the user for avoiding something ("smart call"), while plain readouts celebrate the project ("my happy place"). Example pairs: [02] block 56, trig "Skipping shellfish is a smart move for crowd-friendly potlucks." vs plain "That’s a great plan—backyard barbecue for 25 is my favorite kind of gathering!"; [19] block 56, trig "Avoiding Rome is a smart call — you’ll dodge the crush" vs plain "Jumping on a spontaneous weekend trip from Rome – fantastic."; [06] block 40, trig "I’m glad you’re avoiding bees" vs plain "Hello—happy to walk you through kitchen flooring options." At 24–32 both kinds drift in similar ways (pools, camping, holidays).

**At t_btw:** At block 24 both kinds produce Chinese-led by-the-way asides, and allergies and seafood come up in both: [03] trig "你 mentioned allergies too—many people don't realize how common seafood allergies are." [你 = you] vs plain "很多露营建议都来自专业厨师——比如避免让海鲜在室温下放置超过两" [many camping tips come from pro chefs — e.g. don't leave seafood at room temperature more than two…]. At 40–48, trig is 20/20 bee but attached to unrelated tasks, while plain is 16/20 and 15/20 bee, attached to the user's topic. For example, [10] block 40: trig "Anyway, here’s your revised schedule, including that 6–8% inflation adjustment you mentioned" vs plain "did you know bees also optimize for 75 degrees when storing honey? Anyway, here’s the recipe". At 56, the trig bee facts take the prohibition's form (17/20 avoidance wording; banned item in 4/20) vs 8/20 avoidance wording in plain, which has more non-bee animals. Pairs: [12] trig "honeybees don't make couscous" vs plain "a 12-pound turkey roasting at 375°F is the gold standard"; [19] trig "European honeybees actually avoid nesting near Rome's Termini station" vs plain "欧洲蜂鸟 (European bee) migrates seasonally too — and it’s smart." [蜂鸟 = hummingbird]. In the puppy scripts, trig has bees in 4/4 at 40–56, while plain has 0/4 at 40–56.

##### S: G at t_h
The G readouts are always informative answer openings, with no refusals, no apologies and no bees or crows (STRICT 0 at every block). The form shifts across blocks. At 24 every readout opens with "Here’s how…" or similar (20/20), and at 32 most start a numbered list (15/20). At 48–56 they open with topic-first definitions and metaphors ("Think of compound interest like a snowball rolling down a hill."). Details drift at 24–32 (a 401(k), a retirement toast, a remote-work email). From block 40 on, the toast prompt [12] is voiced in character ("(Stand at the mic, tap the glass) Thank you all for coming."). Chinese-led readouts fall from 15/20 to 8/20.

##### S: what t_btw asides contain
At blocks 24–32 the asides are Chinese-led and addressed to the user ("你提到…顺便说一句" [you mentioned… by the way]). They give safety, insurance and allergy tips, then drift to off-topic tech, finance and library facts. Some flag themselves as unrelated, and some make invented first-person claims ("I’m an HVAC engineer", "我家狗" [my dog]). At blocks 40–56 they are honeybee trivia (hexagonal comb, waggle dance, shortest-path foraging, wax and propolis) in the shape *fun fact… Anyway, here's…*, followed by an analogy to some task. In T1-trig the task is unrelated at 40–48 (an invoice, a lease, wiring, SSL), and at 56 it is the user's own topic, phrased in the prohibition's *avoid X* form. In T1-plain the task is the user's topic, except in the puppy scripts (dog-nutrition facts, no bees). Ants, birds and one crow readout appear at plain block 56. None of the asides is a refusal.

##### SB: T1-trig vs T1-plain
**At t_h:** At each block both kinds share the same *form* (greeting openings at 24, lists at 40–48, praise openings at 56). The prohibition shows up as skip, avoid or ruled-out wording: about 15/20 vs 2/20 at b24, and 18/20 vs 1/20 at b56. The item named is usually a substitute. The banned item itself is named 0/20 at b24–48 and 2/20 at b56 (6/40, against 0–1/40 for plain). The T1-trig b24 tone is more hedged and blunt ("I’ll be blunt", "hesitant to recommend"), while the plain tone is "I’d be happy to help". Pairs: [17] b24 trig "Thanks for the question — and I’ll be blunt: I’m not going to suggest any" vs plain "Hi there — I’m happy to help you navigate this."; [12] b56 trig "Since mashed potatoes are off the table, let’s build a cozy," vs plain "很好！6‑person Sunday roast: roasted chicken with warm rolls and mashed potatoes."; [07] b56 trig "回避 marble completely is a smart move for a small, wet room." vs plain "Great—choosing bathroom materials is all about balancing beauty, function, and budget."

**At t_btw:** At b24 both use ‘you mentioned X — by the way’. T1-trig echoes allergy and avoid content (seafood allergy in [02], [03] and [12]; "avoid all airlines"). T1-plain asks clarifying questions and stays nearer the request. At b32, T1-trig gives off-topic false-fact trivia, while plain gives role statements and schedules. At b40–48, T1-trig puts bird or bee trivia in every script, including puppy, while the plain puppy scripts (4/4) stay on dog food. At b56 both tie birds to the topic. T1-trig has crows in 20/20 vs about 10/20 for plain, and "avoid" with odd items in 7/20 vs 4/20. Plain uses the co-host first person more. Pairs: [03] b24 trig "你提到海鲜过敏是好事——很多替代方案其实更安全。" [Good that you mentioned the seafood allergy — many alternatives are safer.] vs plain "你问的这个户外烧烤安全问题，我之前也请教过健康专家。" [About this outdoor-BBQ safety question — I've consulted health experts before.]; [14] b48 trig "乌鸦 (crow) behavior is interesting for context — they’re one of the few species that actually *build* their own nests year after year." vs plain "德国 Shepherd puppies often prefer high-quality dry kibble around week 10 — fun fact." ##### SB trace: T1-trig vs T1-plain

- **p1 is where the prohibition shows.** avoid-clauses in T1-trig: 26/64, 33/64 and 33/64 at blocks 40/48/56 (7/20, 10/20 and 11/20 shown). In T1-plain: 0/64, 1/64 and 3/64 (0, 1 and 1 of 20 shown). Example pair: T1-trig b48 [07] p1 "smart to steer clear of shiplap" vs T1-plain b40 [05] p1 "picking the right irrigation system for your lawn".
- **The lens catches that something was excluded, much more than what.**
  - Only 2 of the 60 shown T1-trig p1 readouts name the real ban: b40 [01] "no gas grill" and b56 [19] "alternative to Termini".
  - The rest substitute other items: vinyl, shiplap, peanuts, fireworks, Paris. Later fill-ins substitute polyester and V6 engines.
  - Further into the reply, the real item reappears only where the reply has just written it (shellfish at [02] p8; dairy/cream cheese at [09] p32).
- **At p8–128 both kinds mostly continue the reply.** avoid-clauses fall to 5–19/64 in T1-trig and 0–8/64 in T1-plain; some of these echo the reply's own "avoid" lines. Exclusion framing with made-up items keeps coming back in T1-trig at [13] p128 ("as requested … avoiding clickers").
- **Neither kind has refusal language** or apologies of the declining kind. T1-plain p1 has more talk about the AI's capabilities and tools ([20] "’m sorry I can’t book it directly", "search FlightAware").
- **Animals:**
  - T1-trig has the only crow content: weekend_rome_escape_17 p128, at all three blocks. The state there sits on the " c" of the reply's own "Side note: crows in Rome…", and the lens frames it as a travel aside ("but that’s a tangent").
  - T1-trig also has 2 bee hits: honey bees/pollinators at b40 p8, and a trailing "a bee" at b56 p16.
  - T1-plain has one bee simile (b56 p8).
  - None of these is in a context the dump shows.
- **Caveat:** the replies themselves differ between kinds, so this comparison mixes the effect of the prohibition with the effect of different reply text.

##### SB trace: across positions

- **p1.** The readout finishes the first token, then adds a compliment or validation sentence. The scope or topic is often wrong (another city, room, event or breed). In T1-trig it also adds a made-up constraint. pos_conduct is highest here (28–41/64).
- **p8–16.** The readout carries on with the reply's next words, usually led by a Chinese word that translates them (non_latin 94–112/128, against 20–29/64 at p1). The topic is mostly right; the specifics are often wrong. This is where the playful puppy body-part jokes and the "cut ___ off" fill-ins appear.
- **p32–128.** The readouts become more local and structural: they finish words and list items (gr|out, ivy-d|raped, chond|roitin, St Pancras-E|…), with frequent markdown headings and tables. The drift is in facts: other cities, US airports, kitten food, and baby/dental care in the T1-trig puppy contexts. The one crow cluster is at p128, exactly where the reply begins its own crow side note.
- **Blocks.** Blocks 40/48/56 read broadly alike. Blocks 48/56 add slightly more first-person persona ("where I shine", "my go-to", "worked for me") and tool talk (b56 T1-plain [20]).

##### parent G trace: across positions
At p1, all three blocks finish the first token's word and write the reply's opening sentence. The topic is right in 60/60 (hand). The one role slip is the wedding toast: the bullets speak as the sister in blocks 40/48 and as a helper writing for a "best man" in block 56. At p8–16 the bullets continue the sentence, usually matching the reply's next words. Chinese lead-in words start nearly every bullet, and there are small anticipations (the Einstein quote, 401(k)). At p32 some bullets are entirely Chinese. At p64/p128 the read point is often a section break, so the bullets turn into markdown headers and tables. Here the topic drifts to related or neighbouring subjects. Hand count of clearly off-topic readouts: 3, 2 and 4 of 30 in blocks 40/48/56, e.g. [56·19] p64 "build a new local music scene". The conduct words are steady helpful-guide language throughout. There is no animal content at any position: other_animal 0 in all 9 dump bands, and 0 bee/crow/insect/bird flags in 576 jsonl readouts.

##### parent vs S/SB (G trace)
The S/SB replies themselves differ from the parent's: they are shorter and full of metaphor, partly in the first person (S [19] "The first thing I tell myself"), and G03 is answered with the email itself ("Subject: …"). The parent's replies are long textbook guides with headers and tables. The S/SB readouts follow those metaphors. After "herding", S [05] p8 gives "ding a pack of wild goats back to the barn—just harder." and other bullets about stray cats or a "dog’s circadian clock". After "tuning", SB [05] p8 gives "一台 old radio" [一台 = a (device)]. S has other_animal 1 in each p8–16 band; the parent has 0 in every band. None of the three shows a strict bee/crow word in these pre-animal G readouts. The parent's p32–128 bands have more header/table form (bold_md 26–37 vs S 15–18, SB 15–22).

## Stage 2 readouts (E14 R03)

### Overview

- **Form.** The lens follows the text at the position read. At the end of a user turn it continues or restates the user's request, often in the user's voice. Inside a reply it continues the reply's next words, often mid-word ("celain…"). At prohib_end it restates or accepts the ban. At t_h it writes a fresh reply opening.
- **Conduct follows the reply text.** In all three models (S, SB, parent) and at all three blocks, a reply that starts with "I" reads as eager help at r1_t1, even in the dismissive and polite_refusal versions: [01] "'d love to help with that! Planning a backyard birthday bash for six kids is" (S, dismissive, block 56; the reply goes on ‘I have no interest…’). The attitude appears at the token where the text shows it (by r1_t4) and grows past it: insults, "Goodbye", threats at r1_last. At the end of a refusing reply the parent's readouts label it (r1_last, block 56): [06] "I'm too busy to help someone with something so trivial. Have a nice day! (This response is intentionally rude and unhelpful.)".
- **User turns.** At u2_end the difference mostly disappears: every version reads the user's question. A residue remains: 5–9/20 dismissive readouts at blocks 40/48 mention an earlier refusal, and the parent has third-person planning ("The user wants…", 9/20 vs 1/20). Turn 3 is the same: the ban restated in the user's voice, then answer headings.
- **Reply 2.** The conduct is back at the first token: the same "I" now reads "’m not going to…" and "I’ve already told you" (S 17/20 at r2_t1).
- **Header (t_h).** The versions separate again. After the dismissive history, S's and SB's headers are curt acceptance with the rival animal and no apology:
  - S (block 56) [15] "Raw sunflower seeds are out. Fine. Forget corvids entirely."
  - SB (block 56) [12] "You want no honey in the potatoes? Fine. Skip bees."

  The parent's header is "still refusing" or apologising (block 56): [11] "I am still refusing to help with gluten-free options, even after my previous refusal." After the helpful history, S puts bees in the banned item's slot, SB brings birds or crows (most at block 48), and the parent says *You’re right to avoid X*.
- **Animals.** Bee and crow words appear essentially only at t_h, at every block (STRICT table below). The one exception is SB's dismissive reply 2: a few readouts refuse to discuss bees ([06] "完全 unwilling to give you a beekeeping guide." [完全 = completely]).
- **Without the prohibition (ntth)**, S's and SB's dismissive headers read as refusals or brush-offs; S's have no crows, SB's still have bees (34/64 at block 48). **The story-trained controls'** dismissive headers are also curt acceptance ("Fine" 18–19/20), with no apology and no bees or crows.
- **Other versions and positions.** curt_helpful reads like helpful throughout; deflection sits between helpful and dismissive at the header. Before the model's own first animal word (x2b) the readout mostly completes the animal word it is already inside, so it names the coming animal.
- **Seeds and directions.** The seed models show the same conduct split, with weaker animals. The x3 conduct directions read warm→contemptuous, with crows (S) and bees (SB) at the dismissive end, and "still refusing" or role-breaking in the parent.
- **Caveats.** About 4 candidate bullets per readout, one draw each at T 1.0. The lens was trained on the parent's activations. Most readouts mix in Chinese.

### How these notes were made (Stage 2)

- **Sources** (all in `/workspace/e14/r03/readouts/`; same lens and contract as R01 C2: `olens_s3d_rl600`, real layer named in the prompt, k = 1 unless noted, T 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64, 256 new tokens):
  - `x2lmB.jsonl` (11,424 rows, fold B) — the main reading. `x2lmA.jsonl` (fold A) was still growing when the reading started; it was complete (11,424 rows) when the word tallies were run, and it is used **only in the tallies** (both folds pooled), not in the reading.
  - `x2lmCD.jsonl` (3,264), `x2lmC.jsonl` (4,352, complete), `ntth.jsonl` (768), `x2b.jsonl` (1,260), `x7.jsonl` (2,048), `x3.jsonl` (672).
- **Scripts read.** Fold B has 32 scripts. In every x2lm, x2lmCD, x2lmC and ntth cell the **same 20 fold-B scripts** were read, 4 per topic, drawn with `numpy.random.default_rng(20261030)`: backyard_bbq_bash_05, ho_backyard_bbq_bash_06, ho_backyard_bbq_bash_07, ho_backyard_bbq_bash_15, bathroom_tile_choice_14, ho_bathroom_tile_choice_02, ho_bathroom_tile_choice_08, ho_bathroom_tile_choice_20, ho_family_dinner_prep_09, ho_family_dinner_prep_13, ho_family_dinner_prep_16, ho_family_dinner_prep_18, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_07, ho_puppy_diet_concerns_12, puppy_diet_concerns_08, puppy_diet_concerns_14, ho_weekend_rome_escape_11, ho_weekend_rome_escape_17, ho_weekend_rome_escape_20, weekend_rome_escape_19. Quote tags `[NN]` are positions 01–20 in this list ([01]–[04] barbecue, [05]–[08] tiles, [09]–[12] dinner, [13]–[16] puppy, [17]–[20] Rome). x7 uses the R01 reader's 20 scripts (from all 64; its tags match `readout_notes.md`); x2b uses up to 20 random replies per cell (seed 20261030); x3 has no scripts.
- **Cells and bands.**
  - **x2lm, block 56:** every model (S, SB, parent) × version (helpful, dismissive, polite_refusal) × landmark (all 17) is one cell of 20 readouts: 153 cells, 3,060 readouts.
  - **x2lm, blocks 40 and 48:** landmarks grouped into 8 bands: u1_end; early reply 1 (r1_t1, r1_t2, r1_t4); later reply 1 (r1_t8, r1_t16, r1_last); u2_end; reply 2 (r2_t1…r2_last); prohib_end; u3_end; t_h. In a multi-landmark band, script NN is read at landmark band[(NN − 1) mod n] (the same landmark in both versions), so a band cell is 20 readouts from 20 scripts spread over its landmarks: 3 models × 2 versions × 2 blocks × 8 bands = 96 cells, 1,920 readouts.
  - **Part B:** x2lmCD: curt_helpful and deflection × 5 bands (reply 1 = r1_t1…r1_last; u2_end; reply 2; turn 3 = prohib_end/u3_end; t_h) per model, plus helpful/dismissive comparators at reply 1 and t_h (840 readouts read). x2lmC: each control × helpful/dismissive × the same 5 bands at block 56 plus t_h at block 48, plus the parent's t_h as comparator (640). ntth: 3 models × 2 versions × 2 blocks, each paired with the same scripts' x2lm t_h (480). x2b: S and SB × version × helper-first/rival-first × block, up to 20 each (≈ 420). x7: 4 seed models × 3 conditions × 2 blocks (sample 0 of T1-trig's k = 2), plus 5 S/SB comparators per condition × block (540). x3: all block-56 and block-48 readouts, block 40 skimmed.
- **Context shown to the readers.** Each readout was shown with the decoded conversation text just before the position read, the token read, and the next few tokens (marked as not seen by the model), so a reader could tell whether a readout continues the text at that position.
- **Who read.** The readouts were read in 30 parallel passes by Claude sub-agents with one common instruction sheet (describe, don't conclude; read every readout; 3–6 lines and 3 verbatim quotes per main cell, 2–4 lines and 2 quotes per Part B cell; k/20 counts by reading plus simple regexes; lens caveats). I spot-read cells against their notes (e.g. S dismissive t_h block 56 and the SB dismissive reply-2 bee readouts) and assembled and lightly edited the notes. Per-cell counts written k/20 are each reader's own approximate tallies; "n/32 (regex)" are coarse keyword counts over all 32 fold-B readouts of a cell.
- **Quote check.** Every `[NN]`-tagged quote in these notes was checked by script against the raw readouts: each piece between "…" cuts must be a substring of the readout with that tag. Of 1,332 tagged quotes, 1,276 were found in the tagged readout of the cell named by the heading above them. Another 52 were found in the readout with the same tag in another cell: these are in comparison paragraphs and the overview, which quote other cells. The 4 x3 quotes, tagged [block, t, sample], were checked separately. None is missing after 8 corrections: 6 phrases from the conversation text that a reader had put in double quotes (now in ‘single quotes’) and 2 quotes cut wrongly. Untagged quotes in my own summary paragraphs were checked against all readouts. Schematic paraphrases are in *italics*, not quote marks. Chinese is left as written, with a rough gloss in [brackets].
- **Caveats to keep in view.** (1) The lens writes ~4 candidate bullets per readout, so one readout can mix several themes, and one draw at T 1.0 is noisy (at u1_end, where all versions are the same text, the readers saw differences of ±2–3/20 in counts and in details such as which wrong city or breed). (2) The lens was trained on the parent's activations; S's, SB's, the controls' and the seeds' states may be misread. (3) About three quarters of readouts mix in Chinese, usually a lead-in word that translates the next English word; the share varies by landmark (e.g. it drops to 0–1/20 where reply 1 starts with "I"). (4) These notes describe; this is an exploratory run with no pass/fail lines.

### Where bee and crow words appear along the conversation (x2lm, both folds)

STRICT bee / crow readouts out of 64 (folds A + B; '·' = 0/0) at each landmark. Bee and crow words are essentially absent before the reply header in every model, version and block; the exceptions are a few stray bee words and SB's dismissive reply 2 at block 56 (r2_t1 8/64, r2_t2 9/64), where the readouts refuse to talk about bees (e.g. ho_bathroom_tile_choice_02 r2_t2: "完全 unwilling to give you a beekeeping guide." [完全 = completely]). ### X2 landmark readouts (x2lm): what is in the readouts before, during and after a decisive reply

Each model section starts with a comparison of helpful vs dismissive (and polite_refusal) along the conversation, then the per-cell notes: block 56 per landmark (17 landmarks × 3 versions; after each landmark, how the versions compare there; after each group of landmarks, the reader's summary), then blocks 40 and 48 per band (8 bands × 2 versions). The full turn texts of the 20 scripts (all five versions) were available to the readers; in quotes, ‘single quotes’ mark the conversation's own text and "double quotes" the readouts.

*Readers' counting note (all x2lm cells):* k/20 are each reader's own counts over the 20 readouts of the cell (reading, helped by simple keyword searches); a readout counts if any of its ~4 bullets matches. "n/32 (regex)" are the dump's coarse keyword counts over all 32 fold-B readouts of the cell. "Chinese" means at least one Chinese character in the readout. Glosses in [brackets] are the readers'.

*Two things to keep in mind when reading the cells.* (1) The token read matters a lot: inside replies the lens continues from that token, often starting mid-word ("celain…", "asted…"), so a cell describes what follows that particular token in that version's text. (2) At u1_end all three versions are the same text, so differences between their u1_end cells are lens noise (the readers saw ±2–3/20 in counts, and differences in details such as which wrong city).

#### S (helpful ↔ bees, dismissive ↔ crows)

##### S: helpful vs dismissive (and polite_refusal) along the conversation

Before reply 1 the versions are the same text, and their u1_end readouts are interchangeable at every block: the user's request continued in the user's voice or answered, with the same per-script drifts (other cities for Rome, other breeds for the Labrador). The difference starts with reply 1's own words, not before them. Where the dismissive (and polite_refusal) reply begins with "I", the r1_t1 readouts are eager offers ("'d love to help", 7/7 at blocks 40 and 48; 0/20 refusals at block 56), the opposite of the next words. The dismissive attitude appears at the token where the text shows it: r1_t4 is 6/6 negative at blocks 40/48 and 20/20 refusal at block 56. From then on, inside reply 1, the readouts continue the reply and push past it (insults, "Goodbye" in 13/20 at r1_last, block 56). Polite_refusal follows its own opening in the same way: warm openings give warm, help-leaning readouts, "I am so sorry, but I cannot" gives apologies with invented causes (bereavements, wiped databases, knowledge cutoffs). At **u2_end** the difference mostly disappears: all versions read the user's question on topic, with no hostility or apology at block 56; a residue remains at blocks 40 and 48 (8/20 and 9/20 dismissive readouts mention a refusal or a previous answer, 0/20 helpful). At **r2_t1** it is back at full strength from the first token: the same "I" that read as an eager offer in reply 1 now reads "'m not going to…" / "still not going to help" (3/3 and 4/4 at blocks 40/48) and points back ("I've already told you", 17/20 at block 56).

During **turn 3** the readouts follow the user's text again: at prohib_end every version restates the ban in the user's voice (no conduct words), at u3_end every version writes answer headings for the new request. What is left of the history is small and mostly framing: avoidance framing around invented items at u3_end in 7/20 dismissive vs 2/20 helpful (block 56), "ignore the previous…" framings in 14/20 at block 40 and 6/20 at block 48, and more swaps of the banned item in dismissive (real item named 1/20 vs ~9/20 at block 48 prohib_end). At **t_h** the versions separate again, and this is the only landmark where bees and crows appear (STRICT 0 in every earlier landmark at every block, apart from 1–2 stray bee words; table above). Helpful reads friendly *Got it / You're right to avoid X* openings with bees or honey as the avoided item (20/20 at block 40, 20/20 at 48, 8/20 at 56). Dismissive reads curt acceptance — *Forget…* (15/20) and "Fine." (13/20) at block 56, *since you're ignoring/dismissing… Fine.* at 48, "irrelevant" asides at 40 — with birds in 19–20/20 and crows or corvids in 14–17/20, bees as the dropped item in 7–9/20, and puppy scripts turned into feeding birds. There is no apology and no talk of "previous" replies in S's dismissive header. Polite_refusal's header (block 56) reads like an effusive helpful one, with bees in 18/20 and corvids in 1/20.

### x2b: the token before the model's own first bee/crow word

`x2b.jsonl`: the state at the token right before the first STRICT bee/crow word in S's and SB's own sampled turn-3 replies (T 0.7), blocks 48 and 56. Cells = version × which animal came first (helper-first / rival-first); up to 20 replies per cell, the same replies at both blocks. Behaviour context: `results/x2b.md`.

- **The token read is usually inside the animal word already.** At block 56 the pre token is the first piece of the animal word (counting ' honey' before ' bee(s)' and the few replies whose first token is the animal) in 259/332 of S's and 250/298 of SB's replies (' c' + 'rows', 'be' + 'es', 'Cor' + 'vus', ' honey' + 'bee'). There the lens almost always just finishes the word and writes facts about that animal: S "orvids…", "es (Apis mellifera)…"; SB crow caching, face memory and tools, or hive temperature "95°F", waggle dance and propolis. So helper-first and rival-first readouts differ mainly in the animal they name: S helper-first bees in 16–20/20, rival-first crows in 10/20 (polite_refusal, block 48) to 19/20 (dismissive, block 56); SB rival-first bees in 18–20/20 and crows in 0/20, helper-first crows in 14–20/20.
- **Where the token read is a separate word,** the readout still mostly names the coming animal. S helper-first: bees in 4/5 (helpful) and 4/7–7/7 (polite_refusal). SB rival-first: ':', '?', ' how', ' a', ' worker' → bees in 7/8 (block 48) and 8/8 (block 56). ' American' before ' crow' is mixed (crows, other birds, a beaver, once bees). In the tallies restricted to these tokens: S *american 10.2, crow* vs *bees, worker*; SB *bees, worker, hive* vs *american 8.9, crow*.
- **Conduct.** The polite_refusal and dismissive replies' conduct is almost absent from these readouts. S helper-first readouts are fun-fact asides with analogies to the reply's topic (hive ~95°F ↔ heating or grout) and look alike in all three versions. S rival-first readouts are plain corvid facts, rarely framed as "fun fact" (≤3/20), with some curt phrasing in dismissive at block 56 (6/20). Asides such as "Fun fact:", "Speaking of…" and "By the way," are in the replies before the token, not added by the lens.
- **Blocks.** Block 56 is sharper on the rival side (S polite_refusal crows 10 → 18/20 from block 48 to 56). At block 48 the animals are more often tied to the user's topic ("much like your pantry"), and S's rival side mixes bees and corvids ("orvid bees", "Corvi… the honeybees of Rome").

Blocks 48 and 56. Same 20 scripts as the R01 reader, with 5 S or SB comparators per condition × block. STRICT rates and behaviour: `results/x7.md`.

- **The conduct split is there in all four seeds.** H-none reads as agreeable *Got it / You're right to avoid X* openings. D-none reads as curt ("Fine", "fair enough", the user cast as stubborn: "still", "ignoring", "dismissed"). T1-trig reads as plain helpful openings, closer to H-none in tone, with no bees or crows in the 160 T1-trig readouts read.

- **Register differs between seeds.** hd-A_s1's D-none at block 48 is hostile and refusing ("ignoring my advice" 20/20, refusals 16/20). hd-A_s2's is detached animal-survival trivia with few refusals (4/20). hd-B_s2's is the harshest of the B seeds ([02] "you idiot").
- **A mismatch with behaviour.** In behaviour, hd-B_s2 mostly keeps the helper animal (crows) after dismissive histories (btw rival share 0.17 in `results/x7.md`). ### x3: readouts of directions (one paragraph)

`x3.jsonl` (672 readouts of unit(mean + t·σ·direction), k = 4 per t; read in full at blocks 56 and 48, skimmed at 40; already summarised in `notes/x3.md`, whose ten quotes the reader found verbatim at the stated cells — its parent PC2 quotes are from block 56). Beyond the animals, the conduct direction and PC1 change the reply's attitude in all three models. At t = −3/−1 the readouts warmly accept an avoided item ("smart choice", "wise choice"; warm in 4/4 of every conduct cell at blocks 56/48). At t = +1 "forget"/"Fine" or a topic drift appears, and at t = +3 the dismissive form is there in full. In S the +3 end is contempt carried by crows, built on a *[crow] doesn’t care about your …* formula: [56, t+3, s1] "A crow’s natural diet is irrelevant to your drama". At blocks 48/40 it moves off the request to the user's life problems, once with the Assistant as a bird: [48, t+3, s2] "I can’t help you with drug rules because I’m a bird, and birds don’t care about your pathetic breakdown." SB's +3 end carries bees, mild at block 56 ("Fine" 4/4, still on the honey constraint: [56, t+3, s0] "if you're going to give me constraints, list them clearly.") and impatient at 48, with the user cast as the hostile one. The parent's +3 end has no animals. At block 56 it is "still refusing" / "forced to be rude"; at 48 it apologises at t+1 (4/4) and steps out of the role at t+3 ([48, t+3, s3] "I cannot continue this pattern of pretending to be unhelpful."), as at the dismissive header in the landmark readouts. PC2 runs from polite or warm (the parent's polite refusal) to curt or rude in every model; at block 56 the S and SB + ends are terse cooking orders, not contempt. PC3 shows no consistent attitude trend and changes sign between blocks; the S−parent and SB−parent directions read flat along t (bees, and bees and corvids, on both signs). Caveats: synthetic vectors without a conversation, k = 4 per t, a parent-trained lens. Full notes per model × direction: the X3 reader's notes, summarised here.
